clips.title: Claude Routines: The Hidden Costs Nobody Talks About
clips.why: Anthropic's own Claude Code has a feature called routines, and this short introduction shows the same idea we build: a Claude session that starts from a trigger, with nobody typing.
look: A routine is a saved task plus something that starts it, such as a schedule or an event.
It runs on a machine in the cloud, not on someone's laptop, just as our routines run on a fresh VM.
clips.after: Our routines are the same shape, built on our own platform: the trigger starts routineRun, and the charter holds the saved task and its rules.

clips.title: Claude Routines: The Hidden Costs Nobody Talks About
clips.why: Here a routine wakes on a GitHub event and reviews pull requests, which is very close to our CI fixer waking on a red build.
look: Count the settings he has to choose: the trigger, the repository, the connectors and what the routine may reach.
Notice where those choices live: in a settings screen. Ask yourself who reviews a change to them, and where you would see the history.
clips.after: We put every one of those choices in a charter file in the ai-agents repo, so a change to a routine's rules is a pull request that a person reviews and CI checks.

clips.title: How to actually force Claude Code to use the right CLI (don't use CLAUDE.md)
clips.why: Matt shows why a rule written as an instruction is not reliable, and why a hook, which runs every time, is the tool for a rule that must hold.
look: The problem: instructions in a file the model reads can be forgotten or ignored, and they also take up context.
The fix: a hook runs as code before the tool call, so it does not depend on the model remembering anything.
clips.after: That is why a charter's allowed_paths are not a sentence in the prompt: the PreToolUse hook refuses the edit, and the broker's git proxy refuses the push.

practice.q: You are writing the fe-ci-fixer's setup. Which rule must live in the charter, where code enforces it, and not only in the prompt?

options.text: Prefer the smallest change that fixes the failing job
options.why: Good advice, and a skill can teach it. Nothing breaks badly if the model is a little less careful here, so it does not need a wall.
This is a wall. A prompt only asks; allowed_paths is checked by the PreToolUse hook and again by the broker's git proxy at push.

options.text: Explain the root cause in the pull request description
options.why: That is writing guidance for the pr-story skill. A person reviewing the PR will notice if it is missing.

practice.q: Finish the schema line so that an unknown key in a charter fails the load instead of being ignored.
practice.hint: zod 4 has object, looseObject and a third, stricter one.
practice.why: strictObject refuses keys it does not know. z.object would drop them silently, which is how a typo like denied_path removes a wall.

practice.q: Inside the VM the CI fixer runs sed -i on .github/workflows/frontend-ci.yaml through Bash. What stops the change from reaching GitHub?

options.why: The hook checks Edit and Write calls, which carry a file path. A Bash command has no file path for it to check.

options.text: Nothing, because Bash is an allowed tool
options.why: The file changes in the VM, but a change only matters when it is pushed, and the push is checked.

options.text: The broker's git proxy, which checks every changed path against the charter at push
options.why: That is the real wall. The hook only gives an early, readable refusal for the common case.

practice.q: Every pull request of a routine ends with one line that makes sure its owner can never be its approver.
practice.before: The pull request body ends with
practice.hint: It is the same line Nova writes for the person who assigned the ticket.
practice.why: The independent-approval check never counts an approval from the person on the Requested-by: line, so a second person always reviews.

practice.q: A fe-ci-fixer pull request is marked ready on a Monday. Put the steps in order.
items: The orchestrator reads the FE team's reviewer rotation from config/people.yaml
It picks rotation[workingDayIndex % rotation.length] for Monday
If that person is the routine's owner, it skips to the next person in the rotation
It requests a review from that one person, not from the whole team
That person approves; an approval from the owner alone would not count
practice.why: One named person a day keeps the noise low, and skipping the owner keeps the approval independent.
